title: Fractions in Disguise
subject: Maths-2
description: Percentages as fractions in disguise: converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, finding a percentage of a quantity, percentages above 100, comparing proportions, increase and decrease, profit, loss, discount and GST, simple versus compound growth, depreciation and the tricky percentage traps.

questions.question: The word 'per cent' comes from the Latin 'per centum'. What does it mean?
questions.explanation: 'Per centum' means 'by the hundred' or 'out of hundred', so 25% means 25 out of every 100 — 25 marks out of 100, 25 rupees out of 100 rupees, and so on.

questions.question: If we say 50% of a quantity s, which expression does the chapter say this equals?
questions.explanation: 50% means 50 times the unit fraction 1/100 of s, i.e. 50/100 × s = s/2 — half the quantity.

questions.question: Percentages are simply fractions whose denominator is 100.
questions.explanation: The chapter states exactly this: 20% = 20/100 and 33% = 33/100. The '%' sign just hides the denominator 100.

questions.question: According to Kautilya's Arthaśhāstra, what monthly interest 'per cent' was considered just?
questions.explanation: The 4th-century BCE text says 'an interest of a pana and a quarter per month per cent is just'. Five panas was commercial interest, ten prevailed in forests and twenty among sea traders.

questions.question: In the Arthaśhāstra passage quoted in the chapter, which group paid the highest monthly interest per cent?
questions.explanation: Twenty panas per month per cent prevailed among sea traders — the highest rate listed. Forests had ten, commerce five, and the 'just' rate was a pana and a quarter.

questions.question: A 15th-century Italian manuscript writes 'vii p cento'. In today's notation this is
questions.explanation: 'p cento' means per hundred and 'vii' is the Roman numeral 7, so 'vii p cento' is 7%. The chapter lists 'xx p cento' = 20% and 'x p cento' = 10% alongside it.

questions.question: The idea of 'per hundred' can be traced back as early as
questions.explanation: The chapter cites Kautilya's Arthaśhāstra from the 4th century BCE, which already quotes interest 'per month per cent'. The Italian 'p cento' manuscripts are much later (15th century).

questions.question: Kautilya's Arthaśhāstra says the commercial rate of interest was ten panas per month per cent.
questions.explanation: Commercial interest was five panas per month per cent. Ten panas was the rate that 'prevails among forests'.

questions.question: Red paint makes up 3/4 of Surya's deep orange mixture. What percentage of the colour is red?
If red paint is 3/4 of the mixture, what percentage of the colour was made with yellow?
questions.explanation: The whole mixture is 100%. Red is 75%, so yellow is 100% − 75% = 25%, i.e. the remaining 1/4.

questions.question: Surya wants to save 2/5 of his prize money. As a percentage, this is
Express 72/150 as a percentage.
questions.explanation: 72/150 × 100 = 7200/150 = 48. (Simplify first: 72/150 = 12/25 = 48/100.) 72% is the trap of ignoring the denominator.

questions.question: Nandini has 25 marbles, of which 15 are white. What percentage of her marbles are white?
questions.explanation: 15/25 = 60/100 = 60%. 40% is the share of marbles that are NOT white.

questions.question: In a school, 15 of the 80 students walk to school. What percentage of the students walk?
Why can a fraction be turned into a percentage simply by multiplying it by 100?
options: Multiplying by 100 always removes the denominator
Every fraction has a denominator of exactly 100
A fraction is 'per 1' while a percentage is 'per 100'
A percentage is always a whole number below 100
questions.explanation: The chapter says a fraction is of a unit (per 1) while a percentage is per 100, so scaling the fraction up by 100 gives the 'per 100' value. The other claims are false (e.g. 1/3 × 100 = 33.33%).

questions.question: Which of these fractions are equal to 75%? Select all that apply.
7/14 as a percentage is
questions.explanation: 7/14 simplifies to 1/2, which is 50%. Reading the numerator or denominator as the percentage (7% or 14%) is the common slip.

questions.question: The fraction 1/3 expressed as a percentage is exactly 33%.
questions.explanation: 1/3 × 100 = 33.333…%, a non-terminating decimal. 33% is only an approximation; 33% = 33/100 is slightly less than 1/3.

questions.question: 24% written as a fraction in simplest form is
questions.explanation: 24% = 24/100 = 12/50 = 6/25. The chapter also lists 48/200 as another equivalent form.

questions.question: A percentage z% can be expressed by any fraction that is equivalent to z/100.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's general statement: 24% = 24/100 = 12/50 = 6/25 = 48/200, all equivalent.

questions.question: 31% written as a decimal is
questions.explanation: 31% = 31/100 = 0.31. Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places left.

questions.question: 5% as a decimal is
43% as a fraction and a decimal is
questions.explanation: x% = x/100, so 43% = 43/100 = 0.43 (two decimal places because of the hundred).

questions.question: Which statement about 50% of 24 is NOT correct?

questions.explanation: The summary gives this very example: 4/10 = 0.4 = 40/100 = 40%.

questions.question: Which of the following are equal to 1%? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 1% = 1/100 = 0.01. 0.1 and 1/10 are both 10%, ten times larger.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say 100 is a good choice of denominator for percentages?
options: Our number system is base 10, so 100 converts easily to decimals
It is the smallest number that has exactly three digits
Fractions with denominator 100 are always proper fractions
It is the largest number that most people can picture
questions.explanation: Because our number system is base 10, denominators like 10, 100, 1000 fit easily with decimals (31% = 0.31). 100 is also round, large enough for detail yet simple to grasp mentally.

questions.question: 9/34 ≈ 26.47 per cent. Expressed 'per mille' (per 1000) it would be about
questions.explanation: Per mille means per 1000, ten times per cent: 26.47 × 10 = 264.7. The chapter also shows 2.647 'per decem' (per 10).

questions.question: Sugar makes up 9/34 of Variety 1 and 13/45 of Variety 2. Which biscuit is more sugary?
options: Both have an equal share of sugar
questions.explanation: 9/34 ≈ 26.47% and 13/45 ≈ 28.88%, so Variety 2 is more sugary. Comparing just the denominators (34 vs 45) is misleading.

questions.question: On average, about what percentage of the human body is water by weight?
questions.explanation: The 'Percentages Around Us' box states the human body is about 60% water by weight.

questions.question: Ice cream is about what percentage air by volume?
questions.explanation: The chapter's fact box says ice cream is about 30–50% air by volume.

questions.question: About 99.86% of the mass of the Solar System is contained in
questions.explanation: The fact box says 99.86% of the Solar System's mass is in the Sun; all the planets together are a tiny fraction.

questions.question: About 45% of teenagers globally fail to meet the recommendation of one hour of daily physical activity.
questions.explanation: The chapter says OVER 80% of teenagers fail to meet it. 45% is the share of the world's population that watched the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

questions.question: The chapter writes 9/34 as '2.647 per decem'. 'Per decem' means per
questions.explanation: 'Decem' is ten, so per decem = per 10: 9/34 × 10 = 2.647. The chapter remarks that 'per 10' would be too small for many purposes.

questions.question: Madhu ate 120 g of biscuits that are 25% sugar. How much sugar did he eat?
questions.explanation: 25/100 × 120 = 30 g. Or: 25 g per 100 g means 5 g per 20 g, so 30 g per 120 g.

questions.question: Madhav ate 95 g of biscuits with 35% sugar. The amount of sugar he ate is
questions.explanation: 1 g of biscuit has 35/100 g sugar, so 95 g has 35/100 × 95 = 33.25 g.

questions.question: Madhu ate 120 g of 25%-sugar biscuits; Madhav ate 95 g of 35%-sugar biscuits. Who ate more sugar?
options: Madhu, since 120 g is more than 95 g
Both ate exactly the same amount
questions.explanation: Madhu: 25% of 120 = 30 g. Madhav: 35% of 95 = 33.25 g. The higher percentage won here even though Madhav ate fewer biscuits — you must compute, not just compare amounts or percentages.

questions.question: The maximum marks in a test are 75 and an A grade needs 80% or above. The least Zubin must score is
25% of 160 is
questions.explanation: 25% is a quarter, and 160 ÷ 4 = 40.

questions.question: 1% of 1 hour is
questions.explanation: 1 hour = 3600 seconds, and 1% of 3600 = 36 seconds (0.6 minute).

questions.question: 7% of 10 kg is
Surya made 60 ml of deep orange paint in which red is 3/4. How much red paint did he use?
questions.explanation: 3/4 of 60 ml = 45 ml (75% of 60). 15 ml is the yellow part.

questions.question: Which of the following give 40% of 4? Select all that apply.
Using the quarter trick, 25% of 287 is
Using 10% + 5%, 15% of 80 is
questions.explanation: 10% of 80 = 8 and 5% of 80 = 4; 8 + 4 = 12. This uses (10% of y) + (5% of y) = 15% of y.

questions.question: Which is the quickest correct way to find 90% of 460 mentally?
questions.explanation: 90% = 100% − 10%. 10% of 460 is 46, so 90% is 460 − 46 = 414. Subtracting 90 or dividing by 9 confuses the percentage with a number.

questions.question: Which estimate for 2/9 as a percentage uses correct reasoning?
options: 10% of 9 is 0.9 and 20% is 1.8, so 2/9 must be just under 10%
2 out of 9 is about the same as 2 out of 10, so about 2%
Half of 9 is 4.5, half again is 2.25, so 2/9 is under 25%
9 ÷ 2 = 4.5, so 2/9 is approximately 45% of the whole
questions.explanation: The chapter's sidebar reasons exactly this way: 2 is a little less than 2.25 (a quarter of 9), so 2/9 is a little under 25% (it is 22.22%). 20% of 9 is 1.8, so 2/9 is between 20% and 25%.

questions.question: (20% of y) + (5% of y) = 25% of y holds for every value of y.
questions.explanation: (20/100)y + (5/100)y = (25/100)y — the chapter verifies this identity, which is why 25% can be built from 20% and 5%.

questions.question: 10% of a day is shorter than 1% of a week.
questions.explanation: 10% of a day = 2.4 hours (144 min); 1% of a week = 0.07 day = 1.68 hours (about 101 min). So 10% of a day is longer.

questions.question: 3 is what per cent of 300?
questions.explanation: 3/300 = 1/100 = 1%. The common slip is to answer 3% just because the number is 3.

questions.question: What do you notice about 5% of 40 and 40% of 5?
questions.explanation: x% of y = xy/100 = y% of x. Here both are 200/100 = 2. Likewise 25% of 12 = 12% of 25 = 3.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: Millet and water are mixed in the ratio 2:7 to make kanji. What percentage of the mixture is millet?
questions.explanation: Millet : mixture = 2 : 9, so millet is 2/9 × 100 = 22.22%. 28.57% is the error of using 2/7; 77.78% is the water share.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: A student says millet is 2/7 of the kanji because the ratio is 2:7. What is wrong?
options: 2:7 compares millet to water, not millet to the whole mixture
Ratios must always be written with the larger number first
2/7 should have been simplified before converting to a per cent
Percentages cannot be found from ratios, only from fractions
questions.explanation: The whole mixture is 2 + 7 = 9 parts, so millet is 2/9 (22.22%), not 2/7 (28.57%). A ratio of parts must first be converted to part : whole.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: A cyclist has covered 92 km, which is 40% of the Delhi–Agra journey. The total distance is
questions.explanation: 40/100 = 92/d gives d = 92 × 100/40 = 230 km. 138 km is the remaining part, not the total.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: In the cyclist problem (40% = 92 km), how many more kilometres remain to Agra?
questions.explanation: Remaining = 60%. Since 40% is 92 km, 20% is 46 km and 60% is 92 + 46 = 138 km (or 230 − 92).

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: 30% of k is 70. What is 120% of k?

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: 40 is 80% of which number?

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: Workers take 18 days to pick coffee berries in 20% of a plantation. At the same rate, the whole plantation takes
questions.explanation: 20% ↔ 18 days, so 100% ↔ 5 × 18 = 90 days. 72 days is only the remaining 80%.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: A 90-minute badminton session is split warm-up : play : cool-down = 10% : 80% : 10%. How long is play?
questions.explanation: 80% of 90 = 72 minutes; warm-up and cool-down are 9 minutes each.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: To make the halwa recipe for 8 people instead of 4, the proportion of rava must be doubled to 80%.
questions.explanation: The proportions stay 40% : 40% : 20% — only the total quantity doubles. Doubling a percentage would change the recipe itself.

questions.topic: Ratios, Bar Models & Finding the Whole
questions.question: About 90% of the world's population lives in the Northern Hemisphere. With a world population of about 8.2 billion, that is roughly
questions.explanation: 0.9 × 8.2 billion ≈ 7.38 billion ≈ 7.4 billion. 0.82 billion would be 10%.

questions.question: Kishanlal's daily target is ₹5000. On Day 4 he sold ₹6000 worth. What percentage of his target is this?
On Day 5, sales were ₹7800 against a target of ₹5000. The percentage of the target achieved is
250% written as a decimal is
questions.explanation: 250% = 250/100 = 2.5 — two and a half times the original value.

questions.question: A farmer harvested 260 kg last year and 650 kg this year. This year's harvest is what percentage of last year's?
questions.explanation: 650/260 × 100 = 2.5 × 100 = 250%. 150% would be the percentage INCREASE, not the percentage 'of'.

questions.question: 'He achieved 120% of his target' means he achieved
questions.explanation: 120% = 100% + 20%, so sales were the full target plus 20% extra. 'More than' refers to the part above 100%.

questions.question: A percentage can never be greater than 100.
questions.explanation: Percentages greater than 100 are common: 120% of target, 250% of last year's harvest. They simply mean more than the whole reference quantity.

questions.question: Which conversion is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: 28.9% = 28.9/100 = 0.289, not 2.89 (which would be 289%). The others follow x% = x/100 correctly.

questions.question: On Day 1 Kishanlal sold ₹2000 against a ₹5000 target. By what percentage was he short of his target?
questions.explanation: 2000/5000 = 40% achieved, so he was 100% − 40% = 60% short.

questions.question: Eesha scored 42/50 in English and 70/80 in Science. In which test did she do better?
options: English, since she lost fewer marks
Neither — the maxima differ, so no comparison
questions.explanation: 42/50 = 84% and 70/80 = 87.5%. Converting to a common base of 100 makes the comparison fair; counting lost marks ignores the different maxima.

questions.question: 42 marks out of 50 as a percentage is
Why does the chapter convert Eesha's marks to percentages rather than comparing raw marks or marks lost?
options: Percentages are always larger than raw marks
Marks lost cannot be calculated for two tests
Percentages put both scores on the same base of 100
Raw marks are never allowed in comparisons
questions.explanation: With different maximum marks (50 and 80), neither raw marks nor marks lost compare fairly. Percentages express both as 'out of 100'.

questions.question: If Madhu's biscuits have 25% sugar and Madhav's have 35%, Madhav always eats more sugar than Madhu.
questions.explanation: It depends on the amounts eaten. The chapter warns it is inappropriate to compare just percentages when the wholes differ — e.g. 25% of 200 g (50 g) beats 35% of 95 g (33.25 g).

questions.question: 1600 people voted and the winner got 500 votes. What percentage of the total votes did the winner get?
The winner got 500 of 1600 votes. What is the minimum number of candidates who could have stood?
questions.explanation: The other 1100 votes must be split so that nobody gets 500 or more. Two others could hold at most 499 + 499 = 998 < 1100, so at least three others are needed — 4 candidates in all.

questions.question: In the KYC table, the ingredient percentages of one product should add up to 100.
questions.explanation: Each ingredient is a share of the same total weight, so the shares sum to the whole: 100%. The chapter asks you to check this.

questions.question: From the computer-use-by-age graph (highest bar 37%, for men in their twenties), which statements CANNOT be concluded?
options: People in their twenties are the most computer-literate group
There are more people in their twenties than teenagers
Half of the people in their twenties can use computers
Women lag behind men in the ability to use computers
questions.explanation: Group sizes are not shown, so (ii) cannot be concluded; the highest bar is 37%, well short of half, so (iii) is false. The twenties bars are the tallest and every female bar is below the male one, so (i) and (iv) are supported.

questions.question: Tomatoes cost ₹30 per kg three years ago and ₹42 now. The percentage increase is
questions.explanation: Increase = 12; 12/30 × 100 = 40%. 28.6% is the error of dividing by the NEW price 42.

questions.question: A theatre's footfall fell from 160 to 100. The percentage decrease is
In the formula for percentage increase, the amount of increase is divided by
options: The new amount after the change
The sum of old and new amounts
questions.explanation: Percentage increase = increase ÷ original amount × 100. Using the new amount gives a different (wrong) figure — 12/42 instead of 12/30 for the tomatoes.

questions.question: 'The population in 1991 is 165% of that in 1961' and 'the population increased by 65% from 1961 to 1991' mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: If p is the 1961 population, both give 1.65p: 165/100 × p, and p + 0.65p.

questions.question: Petrol cost ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025. The percentage increase is
questions.explanation: Increase = 40; 40/60 × 100 = 66.66%. 40% is the increase divided by 100 (the new price) — the wrong base.

questions.question: A number increased by 20% becomes 90. The number is
questions.explanation: 1.2 × n = 90, so n = 90/1.2 = 75. Subtracting 20% of 90 (giving 72) is the common error.

questions.question: An elephant population p grew by 5% over a decade. The population now is
questions.explanation: New = p + 5% of p = p(1 + 0.05) = 1.05p. p × 0.05 is just the increase; 1.5p would be a 50% rise.

questions.question: 'The demand for cameras has fallen by 85% in the last decade' means the same as
options: The demand now is 85% of the demand a decade ago
The demand now is 15% of the demand a decade ago
The demand a decade ago was 15% of the demand now
The demand a decade ago was 185% of the demand now
questions.explanation: A fall of 85% leaves 100% − 85% = 15% of the old demand. The old demand is 100/15 ≈ 667% of the new, not 185%.

questions.question: Bus fares rose by 3% last year and by 4% this year. The overall increase over the two years is
questions.explanation: The multipliers compound: 1.03 × 1.04 = 1.0712, an overall rise of 7.12%. Adding 3 + 4 = 7 ignores that the 4% applies to the already-raised fare.

questions.question: If footfall falls from 160 to 100 (a 37.5% decrease), then rising from 100 back to 160 is also a 37.5% increase.
questions.explanation: The base changes. Rising from 100 to 160 is an increase of 60/100 = 60%. Percentages are always relative to the starting amount.

questions.question: Kishanlal buys a sweater at ₹300 and sells it for ₹430. His percentage profit is about
questions.explanation: Profit = 130; 130/300 × 100 = 43.3%. Cost price is taken as 100%.

questions.question: The price a shopkeeper quotes to customers before bargaining is called the
questions.explanation: The quoted price (often the MRP) is the marked price; what the customer actually pays is the selling price; what the shopkeeper paid is the cost price.

questions.question: Shambhavi buys notebooks at ₹36 each and sells them with a 20% profit margin. The selling price is
Raghu bought rice at ₹35 per kg and sold 10 kg for ₹300. His percentage loss is about
Manisha buys fertiliser at ₹500 a bag and sells at ₹750. Which statement is NOT correct?
options: Her profit is 50% of the cost price
Her profit is 33.33% of the sale price
Her profit is 25% of the cost price
questions.explanation: 250/500 = 50% on cost and 250/750 = 33.33% on revenue. 25% is neither; the chapter uses this example to show the two bases.

questions.question: Kishanlal's gross profit last month was ₹32,000 and other expenses were ₹8,000. His net profit was
questions.explanation: Net profit = gross profit − expenses = 32,000 − 8,000 = ₹24,000.

questions.question: A shopkeeper buys a geometry box for ₹75 and sells it for ₹110. His profit margin on cost is about
questions.explanation: Profit = 35; 35/75 × 100 = 46.67%. 31.8% is 35/110 (profit on selling price).

questions.question: A carpenter's materials cost ₹475 per chair and he wants a 50% profit margin. He should sell a chair at
A milkman sold two buffaloes for ₹80,000 each, making 5% profit on one and 10% loss on the other. Overall he made
options: Neither a profit nor a loss
questions.explanation: CP₁ = 80000/1.05 ≈ 76,190 and CP₂ = 80000/0.9 ≈ 88,889, total ≈ 1,65,079 against sales of 1,60,000 — a loss of about ₹5,079. The percentages do not cancel because the cost prices differ.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells pencils such that the selling price of 3 pencils equals the cost price of 5. His result is
questions.explanation: Let CP = ₹1 per pencil. SP of 3 = ₹5, so SP per pencil = 5/3; profit per pencil = 2/3 on a cost of 1, i.e. 66.67%.

questions.question: A shop offers 25% off all shirts. Anwar pays how much for a ₹300 shirt?
Samson paid ₹4,40,000 for a car after a 15% discount. The original price was about
questions.explanation: 85% of original = 4,40,000, so original = 4,40,000/0.85 ≈ ₹5,17,647. Adding 15% of 4,40,000 (₹5,06,000) is the wrong-base error.

questions.question: A phone costs ₹8,250 and 18% GST is added. Which expressions give the final price? Select all that apply.
For which purchase amount is the 20% discount better than the flat ₹50 discount?
questions.explanation: 20% of 300 = ₹60 > ₹50. For 180 and 225 the 20% discount (36, 45) is less than 50, and at 250 they tie.

questions.question: Cakely offers '30% + 20%' off. A ₹200 cake there costs
questions.explanation: 30% off: 200 − 60 = 140. Then 20% off ₹140: 140 − 28 = ₹112. The second discount applies to the reduced price.

questions.question: A '30% + 20%' successive discount is the same as a single discount of
questions.explanation: The price becomes 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the original, a 44% discount — less than 50% because the 20% is taken off an already reduced price.

questions.question: Three shops: A 'buy 1 get 1 free', B 'buy 2 get 1 free', C 'buy 3 get 1 free'. The percentage discount at Shop B is
questions.explanation: At B you pay for 2 and receive 3, so 1 of 3 items is free: 33.33%. A gives 50% (1 of 2), C gives 25% (1 of 4).

questions.question: You need exactly 4 items priced ₹100 each. Which shop deal is cheapest?
options: All three deals cost the same
questions.explanation: A: buy 2, get 2 free = ₹200. B: buy 2 get 1 = 3 items, plus one more at ₹100 = ₹300. C: buy 3 get 1 = ₹300.

questions.question: A cooker with MRP ₹1800 at 35% off sells for
questions.explanation: Discount = 35% of 1800 = ₹630, so selling price = 1800 − 630 = ₹1170 (65% of 1800).

questions.question: In an interest rate of '10% p.a.', 'p.a.' stands for
questions.explanation: 'p.a.' is short for per annum, meaning for every year: ₹6000 at 10% p.a. earns ₹600 in a year.

questions.question: ₹6000 is deposited at 10% p.a. The amount after 1 year is
₹6000 at 10% p.a. for 3 years: total received WITHOUT and WITH compounding is
With principal p, rate r (as a decimal) and t terms, the amount WITHOUT compounding is
questions.explanation: Interest each term is pr, so after t terms it is prt and the amount is p + prt = p(1 + rt). p(1 + r)ᵗ is the compounding formula; prt is only the interest.

questions.question: Bank of Yahapur pays 10% p.a. On ₹20,000 for 2 years, compounding gives how much more than no compounding?
questions.explanation: Without: 20,000 × 1.2 = 24,000. With: 20,000 × 1.21 = 24,200. Difference ₹200 — the interest on the first year's ₹2,000 interest.

questions.question: ₹20,000 at 10% for 2 years and at 5% for 4 years give the same amount without compounding but different amounts with compounding.
questions.explanation: Without compounding both add 20% (10 × 2 = 5 × 4) → ₹24,000. With compounding 1.1² = 1.21 but 1.05⁴ ≈ 1.2155, so the 4-year option gives slightly more.

questions.question: Jasmine invests p for 4 years at 6% p.a. without compounding. Which expressions give the total amount after 4 years?
questions.explanation: Amount = p(1 + rt) = p(1 + 0.24) = 1.24p. p × 1.06 × 4 would be four whole principals plus interest, and p × 0.06 × 4 is only the interest.

questions.question: The post office offers 7% p.a. On ₹50,000 for 3 years, compounding gives how much more interest than no compounding?
Giridhar borrows ₹12,500 at 12% p.a. for 3 years without compounding; Raghava borrows the same at 10% p.a. compounded annually. Who pays more interest?
questions.explanation: Giridhar: 12,500 × 0.12 × 3 = ₹4,500. Raghava: 12,500 × 1.331 − 12,500 = ₹4,137.50. Compounding at the lower rate still costs less here.

questions.question: A city of 1.5 crore grows by about 3% every year. After 3 years its population is expected to be about
questions.explanation: 1.5 × 1.03³ = 1.5 × 1.0927 ≈ 1.639 crore. 1.635 crore is the linear estimate 1.5 × 1.09, which ignores compounding.

questions.question: Compounding is an example of exponential growth, while growth without compounding is linear.
questions.explanation: Without compounding the amount rises by the same pr each term (a straight line); with compounding each term multiplies by (1 + r), giving p(1 + r)ᵗ.

questions.question: Why does compounding give a larger final amount than paying the interest out each year?
options: The bank always uses a higher interest rate when it compounds
Interest added back raises the principal, so later interest is bigger
The deposit stays locked with the bank for a longer period
Compounding counts each year's interest twice in the total
questions.explanation: In Option 2 the ₹600 interest is added to the FD, so year 2 earns 10% of ₹6600 = ₹660, year 3 earns ₹726. The rate and period are the same in both options.

questions.question: The reduction in the value of an item due to use and age is called
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the loss of financial value over time — the chapter's example is a bike bought for ₹1,00,000 that sells for less years later.

questions.question: A TV bought for ₹21,000 depreciates by 5% in a year. Its value after one year is
A village's population falls by about 10% every decade. From 1250 now, the expected population after 3 decades is about
questions.explanation: 1250 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 911.25 ≈ 910. 875 is the wrong answer from subtracting 3 × 125 (10% of the original each time).

questions.question: Why is it wrong to find the village population after 3 decades as 1250 − 3 × 125?
options: A decade is 10 years, so each drop must be divided by 10
Each decade's 10% drop is taken on the reduced population
Population figures must always be rounded up, never down
Percentages can only describe increases, not decreases
questions.explanation: The second decade's decrease is 10% of 1125 = 112.5, not 125, and the third is 10% of 1013. Each step multiplies by 0.9.

questions.question: A 10% decrease per decade for three decades is a 30% decrease overall.
questions.explanation: 0.9³ = 0.729, so 72.9% remains — an overall fall of 27.1%, not 30%. Successive percentage changes multiply rather than add.

questions.question: Lab mice change by +5%, −2% and −3% in three successive months from p. Which statements are true?
options: The population after three months is p × 1.05 × 0.98 × 0.97
The population after three months is less than p
The population after three months is exactly p
The population after three months is p × 0.05 × 0.02 × 0.03
questions.explanation: Each month multiplies by (1 + change): 1.05 × 0.98 × 0.97 = 0.99813, slightly less than 1, so the population is a little below p — the +5 and −5 do not cancel exactly.

questions.question: Mice change by +5%, −2% and −3% over three months. The net change is
The length of a rectangle is increased by 10% while the area stays the same. The breadth decreases by exactly
questions.explanation: New breadth = old breadth ÷ 1.1 = 10/11 of the old, a drop of 1/11 ≈ 9.09%. A 10% drop would shrink the area (1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99).

questions.question: Option A: deposit ₹100, get back ₹300. Option B: deposit ₹1000, get back ₹1500. Which gives the higher percentage gain?
questions.explanation: A gains ₹200 on ₹100 = 200%; B gains ₹500 on ₹1000 = 50%. Percentages compare proportions, not absolute amounts.

questions.question: In the same 'Would You Rather' (A: ₹100→₹300, B: ₹1000→₹1500), which option leaves you with more extra money?
questions.explanation: B's gain is ₹500 against A's ₹200, even though A's percentage gain (200%) is higher. The chapter warns to be mindful of proportions versus absolute values.

questions.question: Surbhi marked up her cookware by 50% and then offered a 50% discount. Overall she made
questions.explanation: Price = 1.5x; after 50% off it is 0.75x — three-quarters of what she paid, a 25% loss. The 50% discount is taken on the larger marked price.

questions.question: After the 50% markup and 50% discount, Surbhi sold goods for ₹12,000. She had bought them for
What discount on a 50% marked-up price brings the goods back to exactly the buying price?
questions.explanation: 1.5x × (1 − d) = x gives 1 − d = 2/3, so d = 1/3 = 33.33%. A 50% discount overshoots to 0.75x.

questions.question: Ariba says, 'My marbles are 120% of Arun's.' Arun could correctly say his marbles are
questions.explanation: If Arun has a, Ariba has 1.2a, so a = (1/1.2) × 1.2a = 83.33% of Ariba's. '20% more' does not invert to '20% less'.

questions.question: A shopkeeper prices a product with a 35% profit margin, then gives a 30% discount on that price. He makes
questions.explanation: 1.35 × 0.7 = 0.945 of the cost price, a 5.5% loss. The 30% discount is taken on the larger marked-up price, so it outweighs the 35% markup.

questions.question: In a room of 100 people, 99% are left-handed. How many left-handed people must leave to bring the percentage down to 98%?
questions.explanation: The 1 right-handed person must become 2% of the room, so the room must hold 50 people: 49 left-handers remain and 50 must leave.

questions.question: At a school excursion, 40% of students are from Grade 8, and 60% of those are girls. Grade 8 girls are what percentage of all students?
Which pairs are equal? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: x% of y = xy/100 = y% of x, so the first two pairs are equal (3 and 9). 20% of 50 = 10 but 50% of 25 = 12.5; 10% of 30 = 3 but 30% of 100 = 30.

questions.question: Mathematically 30% + 20% = 50%, so a shop's '30% + 20%' offer is the same as a 50% discount.
questions.explanation: In shopping, '30% + 20%' means successive discounts: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56, only a 44% discount. On a ₹200 cake it is ₹112 versus ₹100 at 50% off.
